planting.note: Plant rooted tip-layered cuttings or divisions in spring into moist, well-drained, sandy to loamy, slightly acidic soil in full sun to light shade; southern dewberry roots naturally wherever its trailing cane tips touch soil.

directions: Plant rooted tip cuttings in moist, well-drained sandy loam in full sun to light shade; southern dewberry is a low, trailing Gulf Coast and Southeastern native bramble that hugs the ground rather than growing upright, with slender, prickly canes that root wherever the tips touch soil. It is among the earliest brambles to flower, opening white blooms as early as late winter in the Deep South, followed by glossy black, sweet-tart drupes ready to pick weeks ahead of upright blackberries. Because canes trail and root freely, give it room to spread or confine it with a mowed border, and expect it to naturalize readily in sunny, sandy fields, roadsides, and open pine woods edges. After fruiting, cut back spent floricanes to tidy the patch and encourage vigorous new primocane growth for next year's crop.

planting.note: Plant rooted softwood cuttings or bare-root nursery stock in spring into well-drained, sandy or loamy, neutral to slightly alkaline soil in full sun; plant two seedlings or two different clones for best fruit set, since fruiting is improved by cross-pollination.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy or loamy soil in full sun; western sandcherry is a low, spreading Great Plains native shrub prized for extreme cold hardiness and drought tolerance well beyond that of most cultivated cherries or plums. White flowers cover the branches in early spring ahead of the leaves, followed by dark purple-black, cherry-plum-flavored fruit that ripens in mid- to late summer and is excellent fresh, dried, or made into jam and wine, though astringency varies by seedling. It is widely used as a dwarfing rootstock and as a parent in cold-hardy plum-cherry hybrids for northern climates where standard stone fruits fail to overwinter reliably. Prune out old, unproductive stems at the base every few years to renew vigor, and expect strong drought tolerance once established, needing supplemental water only during the driest stretches.

planting.note: Plant container-grown shrubs rooted from semi-hardwood cuttings in spring or fall into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in partial shade; holly-leaf sweetspire is slower growing and less cold hardy than the native Virginia sweetspire.

directions: Plant in humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial shade; holly-leaf sweetspire is an evergreen Chinese shrub with glossy, spiny-toothed, holly-like leaves that give year-round structure to a shaded border. In late summer it produces long, slender, pendulous racemes of small greenish-white flowers dangling like tassels or catkins from the branch tips, a bloom time and form unlike almost any other shade shrub and valuable for extending seasonal interest past the usual spring shrub display. It is somewhat less cold hardy and slower to establish than its deciduous North American cousin, Virginia sweetspire, so site it in a sheltered spot out of harsh winter wind in the colder part of its range. Mulch well and water during dry spells in the first two years, after which established plants tolerate normal garden conditions with only moderate care.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container-grown plants in spring or fall into humus-rich, evenly moist, well-drained soil in partial to full shade; this rhizomatous sedge spreads to form a dense groundcover mat.

directions: Plant divisions in humus-rich, evenly moist soil in partial to full shade; creeping broadleaf sedge is an unusual Japanese and Korean woodland sedge with broad, lance-shaped, grass-unlike leaves that arch outward from slender, wiry stems, spreading steadily by rhizomes to form a loose, deciduous groundcover carpet under trees. Inconspicuous flower spikes appear in spring, but the plant is grown almost entirely for its soft-textured, ribbon-like foliage, which turns warm straw-gold in fall before dying back for winter. It tolerates dry shade better than most true grasses and spreads at a manageable, non-aggressive pace, making it useful for underplanting shrubs, softening woodland path edges, and filling in beneath deciduous trees where turf fails. Divide congested patches every three to four years in spring to control spread and renew vigor.

planting.note: Direct sow after last frost once soil has warmed, into average to dry, well-drained soil in full sun to partial shade; purpletop tridens is a widespread Eastern and Midwestern native bunchgrass of old fields, roadsides, and open woodland edges.

directions: Direct sow into average, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; purpletop tridens forms upright, arching clumps of narrow green foliage that stay unremarkable through summer until late summer, when airy, open flower panicles emerge in a distinctive, glossy purple to bronze color that catches low afternoon light beautifully and gives the plant both its common name and its main ornamental season. The foliage and seed heads persist into winter, offering texture, movement, and seed for birds through the colder months. It tolerates drought, dry soil, and considerable shade better than many popular ornamental grasses, and it self-sows modestly in open ground without becoming aggressive in a maintained bed. Cut back old growth in late winter before new shoots emerge to keep the clump tidy for the coming season.

planting.note: Sow or press seed into consistently wet to saturated soil in full sun to partial shade after last frost; rice cutgrass thrives at pond margins, ditches, and other permanently moist to shallowly flooded sites.

directions: Plant in consistently wet to saturated soil, or shallow standing water at the immediate pond edge, in full sun to partial shade; rice cutgrass is a rhizomatous native perennial grass of marshes, wet ditches, and stream banks throughout most of North America, spreading steadily by underground rhizomes to stabilize saturated soil and shorelines. Fine, harshly barbed leaf margins give the plant its common name and deter grazing wildlife and careless handling alike, while airy, drooping seed heads appear in late summer and provide food for waterfowl and songbirds. It is a valuable choice for rain garden basins, bioswales, and pond-margin plantings where its spreading habit helps filter runoff and control erosion in consistently wet ground. Because it spreads aggressively in ideal wet conditions, confine it with a barrier or ample open space rather than placing it in a small, mixed wetland planting.
